# English Presentation Prep — GANA Rebranding

> For live delivery to foreign executives. Short sentences. Full stops, not commas.
> Know the 3 beats, don't memorize word-for-word. When you don't know: say so, then say how you'll find out.

---

## The 3 beats (this is all you must remember)

1. **We sell a promise. We should show what we made instead.**
2. **Here's the proof — 8 registrations, our name, a foreign regulator.**
3. **What's done, we say "made." What's still building, we say "built." We don't blur them.**

If you blank out, just say these three things in your own words. Everything else is detail.

---

## Opening (~90 seconds — read almost as-is)

"Good morning. I'll keep this short.

Today, GANA says one thing to the market: we fight aging. It's true. But it's a promise — and every competitor makes the same promise. The moment we say it, the room asks us to prove it.

So we propose one change. Not to what we do — to how we say it. We stop selling a promise, and we start showing what we've made.

We don't say 'we fight aging.' We say: **from the surface to the cell, we are on the making side.**

And we can prove it. Eight products, registered under our own name, with the Russian federal health authority. Hyaluronic acid, PLLA, PCL, calcium — four different material families — plus a wound dressing. A company that buys ingredients and resells them does not get a list like this. A foreign regulator has already put in writing what we want to say.

That is the whole idea. Everything else in this document is how we do it carefully — and what we have to fix first."

---

## The honesty move (~45 seconds — this is your strongest moment, don't skip it)

"One thing I want to be direct about.

'From surface to cell' has two halves, and they are not in the same place.

The surface — fillers, wound patches — is **done**. Registered. GMP-certified. On the market.

The cell — our gene-therapy plant — is **built, but not yet certified**. cGMP is targeted for 2026.

So we say them differently. Surface: 'we made it.' Cell: 'we built it.' If we blur the two, and someone asks for a certificate we don't have yet, they stop trusting the eight registrations that are real. Split the tense, and both halves stay true."

> Why this wins: a 22-year-old openly separating "proven" from "not yet" reads as senior. It's the opposite of overselling, which is exactly what a skeptical foreign board is bracing for.

---

## Hostile Q&A — the questions they will actually ask

**Q. "The Russian registrations — is that data reliable? Why should we trust it?"**
> "It's not our claim — it's a public database. We pulled the eight registration numbers directly from Roszdravnadzor, the Russian federal health service. The manufacturer name and address match GANA R&D. You can look up each one. That's exactly why we lead with it — it's the one piece of evidence we don't need to be believed on."

**Q. "You say you make at the cellular level, but you have no cGMP. Isn't that overselling?"**
> "That's why we don't say 'we make' for that layer. We say 'we built the plant.' The building is done — 2025. Certification is targeted for 2026. We are deliberately not claiming the certificate before we have it."

**Q. "How does this grow revenue? This looks like a messaging exercise."**
> "Fair. Short term, this isn't a demand-generation plan — it fixes something more basic. For 13 years, our own website has never ranked for our own products. Distributors do. One press release reached 15 outlets; our own site reached no one in 13 years. First we become findable and credible. The revenue plan sits on top of that — and I'd want real input from distributors and clinics before I put revenue numbers in front of you."

**Q. "The CE mark and the patents — are they even yours? I heard another company is involved."**
> "Honest answer: we haven't confirmed that yet. There's a separate company at the same building, and some of those patents may be theirs. We're pulling the corporate registry to settle it before we use any of it externally. Until it's settled, we don't claim it."

**Q. "Why is your capacity listed three different ways — 5,000, 6,000, 200,000 liters?"**
> "Because it was never standardized — and that's a problem we flag ourselves, not one you had to find. The real figure is a 5,000-liter design capacity, single Phase-1 facility. The 200,000 number has no basis, and we're removing it. Step one of this entire plan is: one fact sheet, one number, everywhere."

**Q. "You're the chairman's son. Is this strategy, or a family project?"**  *(may come, may be implied)*
> "None of it rests on my opinion. Every claim in here has a registration number or a due-diligence step behind it. Where I don't have proof, I've marked it unconfirmed. You can check all of it without taking my word for anything."

**Q. "What do you need from us today?"**  *(the good-sign question — have this ready)*
> "Three approvals. One: let us start the cleanup — it costs nothing and it's just correcting wrong labels. Two: let legal confirm who owns the CE mark and the patents. Three: approve the direction — on the condition that step two clears first. And separate from all of it: two registrations expire this month, and those need to be renewed regardless of what we decide today."

---

## If they push and you don't know

Never bluff. Use this exact shape:

> "I don't have that confirmed yet. Here's how we settle it: [registry / due diligence / fact sheet]. Until then, we don't use it externally."

Saying this is a **win**, not a loss. It's the whole posture of the document.

---

## Delivery notes

- Short sentences. Breathe between them. Slow is confident; fast is nervous.
- Clarity beats fluency. They hear non-native English every day. They do not care about your accent.
- It's fine to glance at notes. Senior people read from notes. Reading calmly beats reciting shakily.
- If you lose your place: "Let me go back to the core idea —" then say the 3 beats.
- Land the honesty move deliberately. That's the 10 seconds that makes them take a 22-year-old seriously.
